> of the Name, Blissful Agony, Darkling Trickery, Engling Fury,
> Hag's Wrinkles, Gift of Bellona...
>

Looking at the 10 Ahrimanes decks in the Tournament Winning
Deck Archive, the average number of Engling Furies in them
is 2.5. The most that any deck used was 5. If people are
only putting 2 or 3 in their deck, then it seems to me that
Engling Fury is fine as a rare.

Blessing of the Name and Blissful Agony are not what I would
consider to be general purpose utility cards, and as such I
think it's fine that they're rare. Gift of Bellona got the
tough break that Concealed Weapon was changed with Camarilla
Edition, and Concealed Weapon is the better card for the task.
All of them are inexpensive enough (money wise or trade value
wise) that it shouldn't matter what rarity they are.

Similarly to the !Salubri cards, I've never been concerned
that Hag's Wrinkles is rare. You can argue about the utility,
but acquiring them is very easy. I do use 7 or 8 in my
Anarch Samedi deck, but I'll probably cut a few of them so
I can add a few Forced March.

I can see the frustration with Darkling Trickery. If you do
choose to use it in a deck, you're going to want at least 8
of it, and the effect of the card is very much in line with
most staple, common combat cards.

- Ben Peal

I think there's a pretty significant difference. How many Tzimisce
decks can be build without War Ghouls? Probably quite a few.
War Ghouls are not a Tzimisce staple. They're just one of many
ways you can go with Tzimisce deck.

Engling Furies, however, are so generally useful to an Ahrimane
deck that it doesn't make sense to see it as anything but an
Ahrimane staple. It goes in Ahrimane bleed deck, it goes in the
vote deck, it goes in the combat deck. It might not work in
every deck or be equally necessary but it's hard to argue that
it's a good inclusion in many of them.

There's a big difference between cards like War Ghoul and Embrace
and cards like Engling Fury and Darkling Trickery and that
difference is exactly why the former are fine as rares even if
when they're seen packed in large numbers in certain decks where
the latter should be commons.

> Furthermore, even if these players wanted more Engling Furies,
> they found a way to win 10 tournaments amongst them without
> needing more. That's very telling.

I don't think that's a reason to say Engling Furies should be
rare. If you have cards people _would_ use if they could but
they choose to settle for less due to lack of resources, then
you're creating "good rare" (overpriced) cards. Rich players
in a CCG already have enough of an advantage just by the fact
of their having larger collection without giving them cards
they can afford and poorer players can't. Good rare cards are
ultimately bad for the game, at least when the problem gets
too obnoxious.

Fred

>

I'm not sure what a Ravnos Clown Car deck is but War Ghoul decks
need a certain number of War Ghouls because that's what the deck
does to win. Engling Furies, on the other hand, are marginal
BUT POSITIVE additions to any Ahrimane deck - meaning players
would most likely prefer to include them if they had them but
the difference is somewhat marginal. And they would most likely
prefer to include them in most or all Ahrimane decks.

This is not a good situation just because each Engling Fury
doesn't add a sizable improvement to a deck. It's just like
a Mox cards in Type 1 Magic decks. When pressed to explain
why they're so important, good players often have a hard time.
After all, a Mox Ruby is (for instance), no better than a
basic Mountain in almost every respect except for the
occasional time you draw them in your opening hand (or quite
early) and also have land to put out. Doesn't seem like
all that big a deal, no matter how carefully you explain
it to a beginner. Yet Moxen were still highly sought-after
cards.

The reason is that the advantage, though marginal, is a
pure advantage with very little drawback. Since people will
always strive for any edge in a competition and since there
weren't enough Moxen to put in every single Magic deck that
need them, they became good rare cards. As are Engling
Furies.

Fred

People pay $25 for War Ghouls. They pay $8 for Engling
Furies. If a given deck needs 10 War Ghouls, then you're
looking at $250 in money or trades. There are plenty of
people willing to put in that amount of effort to build a War
Ghoul deck. If that's the case, then it's reasonable to
expect that people would put in $80 of effort to get 10
copies of Engling Fury for an Ahrimanes deck if it was
better to build the deck that way. However, they don't.
They are apparently fine with 1-5 copies.

I did ask Grant Garvin (who has the high count in the TWDA
at 5 copies) if he felt that his deck would be better if he
upped the count of Engling Furies. He said that he did use 6
in a later version (and he owns 8 or 9), but he has concerns
about going higher than that: "That deck requires the untap
and press combat to flow *really* smoothly. When it stalls,
the deck is screwed, and more Engling isn't going to get you
out of that situation."

"I think it is fine as a rare, as while I have been tempted to
shove a ton in the deck, it always would have made me worry
about stalling."

When asked if he owned more than 5 copies of Engling Fury
at the time he won the tournament:

"Yep. I had seven at the time. I cut two from the first draft of
the deck due to it, as expected, jamming during combat when I
wanted a press or crows."

> fact of their having larger collection without giving them cards
> they can afford and poorer players can't. Good rare cards
> are ultimately bad for the game, at least when the problem
> gets too obnoxious.

I do acknowledge that it's a theoretical problem, and one
that has manifested itself in other CCGs. However, I don't
see any evidence at all that it's occuring with Engling Fury.
It's possible that this problem exists for Direct Intervention.

You're making the assumption that people would play with
more copies of Engling Fury if they owned them. In the
example of Grant Garvin, he owns 8 or 9, but doesn't use
all of them in his deck, and he has very sound reasons for
it. Now, for the sake of argument, it's possible that there
exists another kind of Ahrimanes deck that would want
more copies of Engling Fury, but so far nobody's found it,
and I don't think it's a stretch to say that intercept-combat
(the style Grant used) is the best style for them.

- Ben Peal

Nope. This I do not agree with at all. Any "advantage-for-money"
issues are bad. While some forms of advantage-for-money properties
are unavoidable, it doesn't do to simply divide them into "big" and
"small" categories because "small" advantage-for-money characteristics
are not necessary the useful ones.

"Useful" a-f-m properties are ones that bring the company selling it
profit. (There may be other uses for it but I can't think of any.)
So the point is to maximize White Wolf's profit while minimizing the
advantage-for-money - not simply minimizing the advantage. That is,
optimize the ratio of profit-to-moneyed-advantage. Having common
cards that can be used in large numbers is not a very bad thing
because it leaves people the choice of buying a limited number of
packs and doing without decks that need so many of a single common
or buying the same number of packs and trading for the common - thus
giving up other types of decks one could build - or just buying
enough packs to get that many of the particular common. I think
people understand and accept the concept of investing in a CCG to
whatever point makes them happy.

But printing all the components to the standard Ahrimanes decks except
for one generally useful but artificially very rare component is a
lot more frustrating than is worth the profit White Wolf is likely
to be getting from it. There will always be Ahrimanes cards in
existence that simply can never be optimally used, no matter how
customers choose to invest or trade with each other. The better
way to do this is exemplified by Ben's War Ghoul deck: cards that
don't really make decks better but represent unusual and popular
choices for deckbuilding. The other Tzimisce/Vicissitude cards
can still be used for other types of optimized Tzimisce decks. The
War Ghouls themselves can be expensive as hell and not hurt the game
much at all.

Fred

Taste of Vitae:
* Must be played in combat, exposing one's minion to danger
* Must successfully inflict damage in combat, no effect if
Dodged/Prevented
* Must be played at end of a round, Obedience/Strike: Combat ends
thwart it
* Must survive the combat, not a given by any means
* Taste of Vitae is variable in effect, from 0 to any number of blood
gained
* Opposing vampires may be low on blood, nullifying effect
* Can't be played vs non-vampires
* No untap after combat except via another card
* Can be played multiple times in a single combat, once per round

Engling Fury:
* +1 stealth undirected action, exposing vampire to predator and prey
blocks
* Gains 2 blood without fail, regardless of other table considerations
* Free untap if successful
* Is not a hunt and so avoids effects with modify hunting
* Only one Engling Fury per vampire per turn

Pretty clear to me Engling Fury is superior. I'd almost always want EFs
over ToVs if forced to pick. The downsides are small, the largest being
only one per turn per vampire. But ToV has more serious restrictions
while Ahrimanes can fight well, they're not truly a combat clan.

Just fuel for the fire. ;)

Jeff

hear Twincast was $20 prerelease weekend, and still doesn't get used in
almost any tournament level deck. Time Warp comes to mind. These are
all cards which are expensive only sometimes because they were
tournament cards, and always because they are impressive spells. Maybe
I should have said, "Flashiness", or "How impressed will my opponent be
when I play THIS baby". Beta cards cost more than their unlimited
counterparts, which cannot be due to tournament value, since they're
exactly the same cards, just one is more impressive.

impressed enough by the numbers in the bottom corner, but the thing I'm
trying to describe is a quality cards have when, on their own, they get
noticed--either because they change the game significantly when played,
they do something no other card does, or even just because they're
hyped up. These are "big" cards, and players are attracted to these
cards.

Another way to look at it is, the quality that Urza's Bauble lacks
entirely. :)

minor-est effect in existence. That's why I think it's the perfect
example of the opposite of what I'm talking about.)

> - but the cards with the highest

circulation of Engling Fury.

Not worth it. Maybe I don't speak for all players on this, but

advice to keep the proper cards getting to the proper people.

that card they'll need and how difficult it will be to
attain them. If you can demonstrate that they need fewer
than they expect (as the 10 entries in the TWDA do), then
the task of acquiring those cards becomes easier for them.

and what should be common, among the criteria is "what do
players need a few of and what do players need a lot of?"

>

be increased. Also, the supply of Direct Intervention
should be increased if there are no plans to ban/modify

Not everyone is going to want to pay the same amount
for the same thing.

I'm fine with using free market economics to get the
proper cards to the proper people, so long as it doesn't
adversely affect the game environment/balance. In the
case of Engling Fury, I think it has yet to be demonstrated
that its scarcity is hurting the game environment/balance.

cater more to the especially obsessive fan boys who may never even play
the game, but must have a full set of the bridge crew or whatever).
Jyhad has always at least put up the illusion of catering to the
Gruntjobs.

In the Real World, more businesses than not make their money by selling
to the working or lower class. You can sell yachts that .01% of the
population will spend $200k on, or you can sell cheeseburgers that 90%
of the population will spend 69 cents on (per burger, of course). Most
of the time the second business model makes more money. And as the
rich get richer and the poor get poorer, businesses keep sprouting up
to further make money off the poor - stuff like Payday Loans and
Household Finance (which gives out extremely high-interest loans to
people who can barely afford to pay them back).

So, should it be easy to determine how many Engling Furies need to be
printed? Well, enough for Joe Gruntjob to buy a box and get about 5 of
them... How's that?
